KEY MESSAGE 1...

Latest ensembles continue to portray the eastward shift of a
large-scale, mid- to upper-level, northern-stream trough Sunday
into Monday that could bring our next best chance for 
widespread showers. However, the variation within the synoptic 
details of the projected solutions errs to the complexity of the
incoming system and the subsequent uncertainty regarding not 
only the spatial extent of rain that we will receive, but the 
amounts. 

As of this afternoon's update, ensembles seem to be in good
agreement that the primary, mid- to upper-level trough will 
deepen through the Ohio and Tennessee River Valleys tomorrow
into tomorrow night. Short- to medium- range, deterministic 
models take things a step further and indicate a deepening to 
the point of the development of a mid- level, closed low in the 
the Ohio Valley by tomorrow afternoon. As this system tracks
eastward and begins to weaken tomorrow night, a secondary piece
of the northern stream becomes disconnected from the primary
trough due to the persistence and stall of the closed low. These
two troughs largely don't appear to phase as they continue 
eastward towards the East Coast. But, in the outlying scenario
where they do, we now have three scenarios that look to occur: 

Scenario 1: Let this be the favored scenario wherein the two 
troughs do not phase and there are ultimately split axes of
rainfall. In this case, an initial fluid moisture axis will 
move into the region Sunday afternoon, driving an area of
showers for areas to the north and west of Albany. Then, as the
two troughs begin to separate, the moisture axis becomes split
between and northwesterly and southeasterly component, bringing
a break in showers Sunday night. Ultimately, a primary moisture
axis oriented southwest to northeast from the Gulf along the 
East Coast, will largely bypass us to the south, but allow
showers to move back into areas south of Albany by early Monday
morning. The secondary moisture axis will develop along the 
eastern Great Lakes where an area of low pressure will develop 
along a pseudo- stationary boundary, enhancing low- level 
convergence and moisture availability. Another batch of showers
will therefore occur for areas to the north and west of Albany
Monday morning before a surface wave glides along the northern
fringe of the primary trough. This will allow potentially
enhanced rainfall to encroach on the Mid-Hudson Valley and
southwestern New England with lighter showers elsewhere. This
would primarily drive isolated flash flooding concerns for 
portions of the Mid-Hudson Valley and southwest New England. 

Scenario 2: Let this be the scenario wherein the two troughs do
not phase, but the aforementioned surface wave stays to our
south. In this case, the moisture axis would again be split as
in the previous scenario, but this time, rainfall remains
lighter given the better forcing and moisture passing by to our
south. This would ultimately give us lighter rain across the
region and make for very few, if any, flooding concerns. 

Scenario 3: Let this be the outlying scenario wherein the two 
troughs phase. In this case, a fluid moisture axis will align 
from the Gulf into the Northeast along the East Coast. An area 
of low pressure at the surface will develop along a pseudo- 
stationary boundary oriented across the Eastern Great Lakes. An 
axis of heavier rainfall will subsequently develop within our 
area Sunday night into Monday morning, following scattered 
showers Sunday afternoon mainly north and west of Albany. This 
scenario would ultimately give us the most QPF, but heaviest 
amounts and locations of such would depend on the eventual 
orientation of the heavy rain axis. At this time, this scenario
seems to drive isolated flash flooding concerns across the
Capital Region where the axis of heaviest rain looks to set up. 

They key take away here is that we are likely to see some rain
across much of the region Sunday afternoon into Monday. The
uncertainty is exactly how much and where those amounts will
fall. These details will ultimately directly impact the overall
concern and locations for concern of isolated flash flooding. 

KEY MESSAGE 2... 

After this week's historic rainfall, soils are, to no surprise,
overly saturated. In fact, according to the NYS Mesonet soil
moisture analysis, over half of our CWA is at 50-75%, if not
greater, moisture capacity. According to the latest NAEFs, PWATs
are expected to reach 1.5-1.75 by Monday which is 2 STDEVs above
normal. Especially given the first and third scenarios, there 
is definitely potential for some heavier downpours Sunday night
into Monday and, in particular, to places that saw heavy
rainfall previously this week. Therefore, isolated to possibly
even scattered flash flooding is probable. However, as
previously stated, it is going to be highly dependent on the
ultimate set up of the system. Currently, ensembles are
projecting about a medium chance for at least 0.5" of rain
